Where it began

Glenn McGrath was born in Dubbo on 9 February 1970 and grew up in the small town of Narromine, where he first picked up a cricket ball. Doug Walters saw something in the lanky country lad, and McGrath moved to Sydney, where he played his grade cricket with Sutherland.

After that, things happened fast. He first played for New South Wales in 1992–93, and after only eight first-class matches he was in the Australian Test side, making his debut against New Zealand at Perth in 1993.

The player

He played 124 Tests between 1993 and 2007 and took 563 wickets at 21.64, with a best of 8 for 24 and 29 hauls of five in an innings. That places him seventh among all Test wicket-takers. No Australian fast bowler had played 100 Tests until he did it in 2004, and at Lord's in 2005 he collected his 500th wicket.

He was part of the side that won three World Cups in a row, in 1999, 2003 and 2007, and was named player of the tournament at the last of them. His final Test came in Sydney in January 2007, where Australia completed a 5–0 Ashes win and his very last ball in Test cricket brought him a wicket.

What made him special

He was never the quickest. What he had was accuracy, a little movement off the seam and, from a height of 195 cm, awkward bounce. He liked to name his targets before a series, and the plan often worked. Against the West Indies he said he would take Sherwin Campbell and Brian Lara with consecutive balls for his 299th and 300th wickets. He did, then removed Jimmy Adams to complete a hat-trick. Mike Atherton fell to him 19 times. He also began the habit of a bowler holding the ball up to the crowd after taking five.

Batting was another matter. He was out first ball on his Test debut, and his 641 Test runs came at 7.37. Steve Waugh coached him patiently for years, and in November 2004 at the Gabba he made 61, adding 114 for the last wicket with Jason Gillespie while his team-mates cheered every run.

Away from the middle

He had a happy summer with Worcestershire in 2000, taking 80 wickets at 13.21, and bowled for Delhi in the first IPL season in 2008. Later he followed Dennis Lillee as director of the MRF Pace Foundation in Chennai, passing on his craft to young fast bowlers.

In 2002 he and his wife Jane founded the McGrath Foundation, which pays for specialist nurses in communities right across Australia. From 2007 the third day of the Sydney Test became Jane McGrath Day. He received the Allan Border Medal in 2000, was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 2008 and an Officer in 2024, and entered the ICC Hall of Fame in 2013. Narromine put up a statue of him in 2009.

And finally

Before the 2005 Ashes he forecast a 5–0 Australian win and promised to go home by boat if England won. England took the series 2–1. Undaunted, he predicted 5–0 again for the next Ashes, in 2006–07, and this time he was exactly right. Accuracy, it seems, was never a problem; it just took him two goes.
